title: Two Mussar schools
hookLine: Novarodok taught fierce self-scrutiny; Slabodka taught human greatness
last: HOLINESS: BEGUN BY EFFORT, FINISHED AS A GIFT.

cards: Two coaches watch the same young runner stumble. The first walks over and says: let's look hard at what went wrong, every step of it, and not flinch. The second says: do you have any idea what you're capable of?
Both want the runner to get better. Both love the sport. They just start from opposite ends.
The Mussar movement Rabbi Israel Salanter began, which this path met in year three, grew into schools like that, each with its own yeshiva and its own temperament.

teach.b: First, Novarodok. Its founder, Rabbi Yosef Yozel Horowitz, is remembered as the Alter, the elder, of Novarodok.
His school taught fierce self-scrutiny: look straight at your own motives, especially the hidden wish to be admired, and don't look away. Second, how fierce.
Stories are told of Novarodok students sent into a shop to ask, out loud, for something it plainly didn't sell.
The point, as the stories tell it, was to stand there while people laughed, and learn that their opinion didn't have to run your life. Whether every story happened just that way, nobody can promise.
The aim behind them is clear: freedom from the crowd. Third, Slabodka. Its leader, Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel, was also called the Alter, of Slabodka.

teach.h: SLABODKA: THE GREATNESS OF THE HUMAN.
teach.b: His school started from the other end, with a phrase that became its banner: gadlut ha-adam, the greatness of the human being.
The root is in Genesis: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him."
Slabodka students learned to see that image in themselves and in everyone, and to dress, speak and carry themselves with the dignity it deserves. Fourth, the shared ground.
Both schools came out of the same movement and asked the same question: how does a person actually change? Novarodok said: see your smallness honestly.
Slabodka said: see your greatness, and you won't want to act small. Some students of Mussar start from one door, some from the other, and some walk through both.

how: Mussar study today draws on both schools: some groups emphasize a hard, honest look at one's motives, others begin from the dignity of every person created in God's image, and many teachers mix the two.

games.why: as the stories tell it, the point was freedom from the crowd: to stand there while people laughed and stay yourself.

practice: Let one true, good thing about you come to mind, not a trophy but something quieter: the way you show up for a friend, a patience you didn't used to have, a stubborn honesty. Name it plainly, without a joke to soften it.
Then ask Slabodka's question: if that greatness is real, what small habit is beneath you? If you pray, give thanks for it in your own words.
